title: Tim Berners-Lee: Connecting the World with One Click
source_book: Information Management: A Proposal (CERN Report) & Weaving the Web
source_chapter: CERN Archive March 1989 & Chapter 1: Enquire Within Upon Everything
authenticity_note: Based on Tim Berners-Lee's original March 1989 CERN proposal annotated by his supervisor Mike Sendall as 'Vague but exciting...', creating HTML, HTTP, URLs, and the first web browser/server.
summary: In 1989, at CERN in Switzerland, British software engineer Tim Berners-Lee grew frustrated that scientists could not share documents across different computer systems. He invented HTML, HTTP, and the World Wide Web—and gave his invention to humanity completely free, changing human civilization forever.
content:
In 1989, the European particle physics laboratory CERN in Geneva, Switzerland, was a bubbling hive of brilliant international scientists. But CERN had a maddening logistical nightmare: thousands of researchers from dozens of countries brought their own incompatible computers, operating systems, and disk formats. If a scientist in Geneva wanted to read data gathered by a colleague in Rome, they often had to physically log into a separate terminal or mail a magnetic tape!

British computer programmer Tim Berners-Lee envisioned a radical solution. Inspired by a Victorian household encyclopedia called *Enquire Within Upon Everything*, Berners-Lee proposed linking documents together using 'hypertext'—clickable words that instantly jump across networks from one file to another.

In March 1989, Berners-Lee handed his supervisor Mike Sendall a proposal entitled *Information Management: A Proposal*. Sendall read the document, chuckled, and scribbled four immortal words on the cover: *"Vague but exciting..."*

Given the green light, Berners-Lee worked furiously on a black NeXT computer in late 1990. In just a few months, he created the three fundamental pillars of the web:
1. **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language): the language to format pages.
2. **URI / URL** (Uniform Resource Identifier): universal addresses for every document on Earth.
3. **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): the rules for servers to send pages to browsers.

By Christmas 1990, Berners-Lee launched the world's very first website: `http://info.cern.ch`, running on his desktop computer with a handwritten red sticker warning: *"This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!"*

Berners-Lee could have patented the web and become the wealthiest individual on Earth. Instead, in April 1993, he convinced CERN to release the entire source code into the public domain royalty-free forever. His selfless gift connected billions of minds, democratized human knowledge, and created the modern global civilization.
